title: Feature Scaling
text:
Standardization (z-score normalization)
\[z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]
Where:

\(z\) is the calculated z-score
\(x\) is the original data value
\(\mu\) is the population mean (average) of the dataset
\(\sigma\) is the population standard deviation of the dataset

The mean(\(\mu\)) of Age column is 34.5 and the standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) is 17.68. If we use these two value and calculate the Scaled Age column using the formula, we will get the actual standized value.

There is a fixed rule for this standardized technique that is the mean of standardized values (in this case Scaled Age) will be 0 and the standardard deviation will be 1.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.fit(x_train)

x_train_scaled = pd.DataFrame(scaler.transform(x_train), columns=x_train.columns)

The Golden Rule: Why don’t we fit the test data?
You might wonder why there isn’t a line of code saying scaler.fit(x_test).
In machine learning, your test data represents “unseen future data.” If you calculate the mean and standard deviation using the test data, you are allowing information about your test set to “leak” into your model before you actually test it. This is called Data Leakage, and it will give you a falsely high accuracy score that will crash when deployed in the real world.
By only fitting on x_train, you ensure your model is scaling the “future” data based solely on the rules it learned from the past.

Why scaling is so important?
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is highly sensitive to Scaling. It is a distance-based algorithm. It calculates the Euclidean distance between data points to find the nearest neighbors.
In our dataset:
* Age ranges from ~18 to 60.
* EstimatedSalary ranges from ~15,000 to 150,000.
When calculating distance: \(\sqrt{(Age_1 - Age_2)^2 + (Salary_1 - Salary_2)^2}\)
Because the Salary values are so much larger, the \((Salary_1 - Salary_2)^2\) term completely dominates the distance. The model effectively ignores the Age column. Scaling brings both to the same range, allowing the model to consider both features equally.

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
knn_scaled = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)

knn.fit(x_train, y_train)
knn_scaled.fit(x_train_scaled, y_train)

y_pred = knn.predict(x_test)
y_pred_scaled = knn_scaled.predict(x_test_scaled)

print("Actual", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("Scaled", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_scaled))

Actual 0.825
Scaled 0.9166666666666666


As you can see, for distance-based algorithms like KNN, Scaling is not just a ‘good practice’—it’s mandatory for the model to work correctly.


Models that do NOT need Scaling
On the other hand, Tree-based algorithms (like Decision Trees, Random Forests, XGBoost) are completely immune to the scale of the features.
A decision tree splits data based on simple rules (e.g., “Is Age > 40?”). The mathematical magnitude of the number doesn’t affect the split at all. Let’s see this in action using a Decision Tree Classifier:

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)
dt_scaled = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0)

dt.fit(x_train, y_train)
dt_scaled.fit(x_train_scaled, y_train)

y_pred_dt = dt.predict(x_test)
y_pred_dt_scaled = dt_scaled.predict(x_test_scaled)

print("Actual", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_dt))
print("Scaled", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_dt_scaled))

Actual 0.875
Scaled 0.875

title: Feature Scaling
text:
Min-Max Scaling (Normalization)
Min-Max Scaling is a data preprocessing technique that transforms numerical features to fall within a specific, bounded range—typically between exactly 0 and 1. By compressing or stretching the data while maintaining its original distribution shape, it prevents variables with inherently larger numbers from dominating those with smaller scales. This is especially important for distance-based machine learning algorithms like K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) or neural networks.

The Formula
To calculate the scaled value of a data point, you subtract the feature’s minimum value and divide by its range:
\[X_{scaled} = \frac{X - X_{min}}{X_{max} - X_{min}}\]
Where:

\(X\) is the original data point.
\(X_{min}\) is the minimum value within that feature column.
\(X_{max}\) is the maximum value within that feature column.
\(X_{scaled}\) is the newly normalized value.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Most developers I know are extraordinarily good at thinking in systems—at decomposing problems,
spotting edge cases, and reasoning about trade-offs. Yet the same people often tell me they
“can’t write.” I think they’ve confused polish with clarity, and that’s a fixable mistake.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Writing Is Thinking Made Visible
When you write, you’re not transcribing thoughts that are already finished. You’re discovering
what you actually think. The discipline of forming a sentence forces you to choose between
ideas, discard the weak ones, and commit to the strong ones.



A developer writing at a desk



“I write to find out what I think.”
— Joan Didion

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Five Reasons Developers Should Blog

Teaching solidifies understanding. The “Feynman technique”—explain a concept simply until
you can’t—exposes every gap in your knowledge faster than any test.
Your future self will thank you. A post explaining how you solved a tricky CORS issue is a
personal reference you’ll return to, and it’ll save someone else three hours of debugging.
Writing compounds. Thirty posts means thirty permanent search-indexed artifacts of your
expertise. That’s a form of leverage most developers ignore entirely.
It builds professional credibility. Recruiters, hiring managers, and peers read blogs.
A thoughtful post demonstrates judgment in a way a résumé cannot.
It builds the habit of finishing things. A blog post has a clear done state. That’s
rarer and more valuable than it sounds.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
section: Common Objections (and Why They Don’t Hold)
text:
Common Objections (and Why They Don’t Hold)
“I don’t have anything original to say.” You don’t need to be first. You need to be useful.
A beginner’s explanation of a hard topic is often more helpful than the expert’s, because you
remember what confused you.
“No one will read it.” Write for one person: your past self, six months ago. If it would
have helped you then, publish it.
“I don’t have time.” A 400-word post once a month is better than nothing. Write rough. Edit
once. Ship.

But what about the categorical features? We will use the Chi-Square test to check the correlation between the categorical features.
In statistics, the Null Hypothesis assumes that the two columns have no relationship at all. We assume the alpha(Significance level) to be 0.05. Here alpha is the threshold we set for rejecting the null hypothesis.
P-value is the result of the chi-square test. If the p-value is less than alpha, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant association between the feature and the target variable. Otherwise, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, suggesting no significant association between the feature and the target variable. In that case, we may consider dropping the feature from our model.

from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

chi2_results = []

for feature in cat_cols:
    crosstab = pd.crosstab(df['case_status'], df[feature])
    chi2, p_value, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(crosstab)
    if p_value < 0.05: # Checking significance level (alpha = 0.05)
        decision = 'Reject Null (Significant Relationship)'
    else:
        decision = 'Fail to Reject (No Relationship)'
        
    chi2_results.append({
        'Feature': feature,
        'P-Value': p_value, 
        'Hypothesis Result': decision
    })

Types of EDA

Univariate Analysis: This type of analysis focuses on a single variable. It includes techniques such as frequency distribution, measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), and measures of dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation).
Bivariate Analysis: This analysis examines the relationship between two variables. Common techniques include scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and cross-tabulations.
Multivariate Analysis: This type of analysis involves more than two variables. Techniques include multiple regression, principal component analysis (PCA), and cluster analysis.

title: Handling Categorical Feature
text:
Categorical features are variables that contain text labels or categories rather than numerical values (for example: “Color,” “City,” or “Size”).
The core challenge with categorical data is that most machine learning algorithms are rooted in mathematics. They require numerical inputs to calculate equations, distances, and probabilities. If you try to feed raw text like “New York” or “Red” into a model, it will throw an error. Therefore, handling categorical features is the process of translating these text categories into a numerical format that an algorithm can understand, without losing the underlying information.


There are two primary ways to convert categorical data into numbers, depending on whether the data has a natural order:
1. Ordinal Encoding (For Ordered Categories)
Use this when your categories have a clear, logical ranking or hierarchy. The technique assigns a distinct integer to each category based on its order.

Example: A “Size” column with values Small, Medium, Large.
Transformation: Small becomes 1, Medium becomes 2, and Large becomes 3. The model understands that 3 is greater than 1, preserving the inherent rank.

2. One-Hot Encoding (For Unordered/Nominal Categories)
Use this when your categories do not have any mathematical relationship or ranking to one another. Instead of assigning a single number (which might trick the model into thinking one category is “greater” than another), One-Hot Encoding creates a new, separate column for every unique category. Each column is filled with 1 (if the category is present) or 0 (if it is not).

Example: A “Color” column with values Red, Green, Blue.
Transformation: It splits into three new columns: Is_Red, Is_Green, and Is_Blue. A red item would have a 1 in the Is_Red column and a 0 in the others.

The Drawbacks of One-Hot Encoding
While it is the standard for nominal data, One-Hot Encoding has four major pitfalls:

Extreme Sparsity: It generates a dataset filled almost entirely with zeroes, which consumes excessive memory and slows down training times.
The Dummy Variable Trap: It introduces perfect multicollinearity (features predicting each other), which will break linear models unless you drop one of the encoded columns.

title: Introduction to Feature Engineering
text:
Feature engineering is the process of using domain knowledge to extract features from raw data. These features can be used to improve the performance of machine learning algorithms.
At first, we do Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) to understand the data and identify the problem we are trying to solve. These problems are solved in the Feature Engineering step.
The features are also known as columns or independent variables.
There is a concept called “GIGO” which stands for “Garbage In, Garbage Out”. That means if we have a poor model and we feed it with good data, we will get good results. But if we have a good model and we feed it with poor data, we will get poor results.
So, the steps are: Data Loading -> EDA -> Feature Engineering -> Model Training
Let’s try to understand what are in the feature engineering.
Feature Engineering
├── Feature Transformation
│   ├── Missing Value Handling
│   ├── Handling Categorical Feature
│   ├── Outlier Detection
│   └── Feature Scaling
├── Feature Construction
├── Feature Selection
└── Feature Extraction
Here is a high-level overview of the feature engineering process.



Missing Value Handling:
Here is an image for example.



Missing Value Handling.png


In the image, we can see that some cells values are NaN which means this dataset contains missing values. The most popular way to handle missing values is to fill them with the mean. In the image, we can fill the missing values with the mean that is 26.0. Sometimes there are outliers in the dataset. In that case, we can fill the missing values with the median. The median is less affected by outliers than the mean. We will see them in practical later.
Handling Categorical Feature:
Here is an image for example.



Handling Categorical Feature.png


We can not use categorical features directly in machine learning algorithms. We need to convert them into numerical features. The most popular way to handle categorical features is to use one-hot encoding. The image shows the one-hot encoding. There are other ways to handle categorical data. We will dicuss more later.
Outlier Detection:
Here is an image for example.



Outlier Detection.png


In the image, we can see that there are some outliers in the left graph. Thats why the linear regression line is not fitting well. After removing the outliers(right graph), the linear regression line is fitting well. So they must be removed by the IQR method for better performance of some models.
Feature Scaling:



Feature Scaling.png


If we look at this data, we can see that the value range of the Age column is very lower than the value range of the Salary column. So the dataset is not scaled. If we use this dataset to train the models that works on distance, the model will give more importance to the Salary column than the Age column. So we need to scale the dataset which is not expected. There is another problem with gradient descent(which is used for reducing the loss). If we use this dataset, the gradient descent will not converge because of the different value ranges. So we need to scale the dataset.




We can create new features from the existing features by feature construction.



Feature Construction.png


Look at this titanic dataset. We can see that there are two features ‘SibSp’ and ‘Parch’. Suppose we want to create a new feature ‘Family’ which is the sum of ‘SibSp’ and ‘Parch’. By using this new feature, we can create a new feature ‘FamilySize’ which is a categorical feature. If ‘Family’ == 1, then ‘FamilySize’ = ‘Alone’, if ‘Family’ > 1 and ‘Family’ <= 4, then ‘FamilySize’ = ‘Medium’, if ‘Family’ > 4, then ‘FamilySize’ = ‘Large’. This is an example of feature construction. This helps us to reduce the curse of dimensionality.



We will use MNIST handwritten digit dataset for this example.



Feature Selection1.png





Feature Selection2.png


In the image, we can see that there are so many features we don’t need. We can select the most important features by using feature selection and omit other features. This helps us to reduce the curse of dimensionality and improve the performance of the model.



Suppose we have two independent features Number of Rooms and Number of Bedrooms and we have a target variable Price. We have to predict the price of a house based on the number of rooms and bedrooms. Our target is to remove the two features and create a new feature Area. There may be a confusion between feature construction and feature extraction. The difference is that in feature construction, we create new features from the existing features by calculation, but in feature extraction, we try to maintain the meaning of the removed features with the new feature.
